name: Redis
summary: An in-memory data-structure server: the default cache, and also queues, counters and leaderboards.
intro: Redis keeps its whole dataset in RAM and answers commands over a simple TCP protocol, which is why reads and writes take well under a millisecond. Values aren’t just strings: there are hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and more, each with atomic commands such as `INCR`, `ZADD` or `XADD`. So one server can be a cache, a rate limiter, a leaderboard and a job queue. Redis 8 also folded JSON, time series, probabilistic types, the query engine and a new vector-set type into the core.

Durability is optional. RDB writes periodic snapshots. The append-only file (AOF) logs every write and, with the default once-a-second `fsync`, can lose about one second of data in a crash. Redis Cluster shards keys across nodes using 16,384 hash slots. Licensing has changed twice. Up to 7.2 Redis was BSD. In March 2024 version 7.4 moved to a choice of RSALv2 or SSPLv1, and the Linux Foundation forked 7.2.4 as Valkey, which stays BSD and is backed by AWS, Google, Oracle and others. Redis 8, released in May 2025, added the OSI-approved AGPLv3 as a third option.
strengths: Sub-millisecond reads and writes from memory
Rich data structures with atomic operations cover caching, counters, queues and rankings
Simple to run, with client libraries for most languages and managed services such as Amazon ElastiCache and Google Cloud Memorystore
Redis Cluster shards data and fails over automatically
limits: The dataset has to fit in RAM, which costs far more per GB than disk
Even with AOF, the default setting can lose about a second of writes, and Redis Cluster can lose acknowledged writes during failover
Multi-key commands in a cluster work only when all keys share a hash slot, which means designing keys with hash tags
The licence history is complicated; teams that avoid AGPL often pick the BSD-licensed Valkey fork

sections.title: Using Redis as a queue
sections.intro: Redis has no queue type, but three of its features behave like one, with different answers to what happens when a consumer crashes. Job-queue libraries such as RQ for Python and Bull for Node.js build on them.

rows.label: List
values: `LPUSH` to add; `RPOP`, or `BRPOP` to block until something arrives
The message is lost: it left the list when it was popped

rows.label: List with a processing list
values: `LMOVE` (or blocking `BLMOVE`) pops it and pushes it onto a processing list in one step; `LREM` removes it when done
It stays in the processing list; a separate monitor pushes items that sit there too long back onto the queue

rows.label: Stream with a consumer group
values: `XADD` to append; `XREADGROUP … >` to read new entries; `XACK` when done
It stays in the group’s pending entries list; the consumer rereads it from ID `0`, or another takes it over with `XAUTOCLAIM` (at least once)
One consumer in each group; every group gets every entry, and entries stay until the stream is trimmed

rows.label: Pub/sub
values: The message is lost: delivery is at most once and nothing is stored
Every subscriber connected at that moment

notes: `LMOVE` arrived in Redis 6.2 and replaces the deprecated `RPOPLPUSH`.

story: In 2009, Salvatore Sanfilippo (known as antirez) was trying to scale LLOOGG, a real-time web log analyzer run by his Italian startup. Every read and write in its MySQL backend went to disk, and as traffic grew the database couldn’t keep up. He prototyped a small in-memory server in Tcl, the “LLOOGG Memory DB”, which already stored strings and lists, then rewrote it in C. He called it Redis, for REmote DIctionary Server.

Once it worked, he decided to share it, and when it was posted to Hacker News in February 2009 it drew only a few comments, half of them his own replies. Developers caught on anyway: in November 2009 GitHub announced Resque, its Redis-backed job queue. VMware hired Sanfilippo in March 2010 to work on Redis full time. Pivotal later took over as sponsor, and in July 2015 Sanfilippo moved to Redis Labs (now Redis Ltd.). Redis 3.0, released that April, added Redis Cluster.

In June 2020 Sanfilippo stepped back as maintainer, writing that he “never wanted to be a software maintainer”. In March 2024 Redis Ltd. moved the core from the BSD licence to RSALv2 and SSPLv1, and eight days later the Linux Foundation forked the last BSD version as Valkey. Sanfilippo rejoined the company in December 2024, argued for the AGPLv3, and Redis 8 added it as a third licence option in May 2025.

choices.choice: Keep the whole dataset in memory
choices.why: Serving everything from RAM gives very fast reads and writes, at the cost of datasets no bigger than memory. Structures in memory are also much simpler to manipulate than on disk, so Redis does a lot with little internal complexity. An early experiment with virtual memory for bigger datasets was dropped.

choices.choice: Expose data structures, not just strings
choices.why: Sanfilippo preferred working with lists and hash tables directly. Values are lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets with atomic commands on each, so a counter or a queue needs no locking in the application.

Redis is usually limited by memory or network, not CPU, and a single instance can serve around a million requests per second with pipelining. A single thread makes every command atomic; to use more cores, you run more instances.

To save, Redis forks a child that shares memory pages copy-on-write and writes them out while the parent keeps serving. The on-disk formats never need random access, so they’re compact and always written append-only.

timeline.text: Built to scale LLOOGG; released as open source in February
VMware hires Sanfilippo to work on Redis full time
Redis 3.0 ships Redis Cluster; Redis Labs becomes sponsor
Core moves to RSALv2/SSPLv1; Linux Foundation forks Valkey
Redis 8 adds the AGPLv3 option and vector sets
